item.title: MAGIC launches AIMM 2026, offers Rs 7 lakh in prizes for AI innovations
item.description: Got an AI idea? MAGIC has opened applications for AIMM 2026, offering startups, MSMEs, students and researchers a chance to win Rs 7 lakh, with potential seed funding and incubation support.
item.content:encoded:
Artificial intelligence is finding applications across industries, but turning an idea into a solution that businesses and communities can actually use takes more than technology. It requires testing, development and access to the right support.

The Marathwada Accelerator for Growth and Incubation Council (MAGIC) is inviting innovators across India to take on this challenge through the eighth edition of its national innovation competition, AIMM 2026.

Themed Artificial Intelligence for Manufacturing and Mankind, the competition aims to encourage the development of AI-based solutions to real-world problems in manufacturing, industry and society.

Startups, aspiring entrepreneurs, micro, small and medium enterprises (MSMEs), students and research teams can apply. The last date for submissions is December 7, 2026.

Two stages for AI innovations

AIMM 2026 will have two categories, giving participants an opportunity to present ideas at different stages of development.

The first category is for innovations at the minimum viable product (MVP) stage, including concepts and proof-of-concept projects. The second is aimed at products that are already available in the market and generating revenue.

The distinction allows both early-stage innovators and businesses with market-ready solutions to participate. Rather than focusing only on ideas, the competition also aims to encourage the development of products that can be taken to market and expanded.

Winners can access funding and incubation support

The competition carries total cash prizes worth Rs 7 lakh. Selected innovations may also receive seed funding support and an opportunity to access incubation through MAGIC.

The additional support is intended to help participants take their ideas beyond the competition, work towards commercial products and explore opportunities for market expansion.

Through AIMM 2026, MAGIC wants to encourage the adoption of AI across industries and support technology-led solutions that address practical challenges. Bringing startups, businesses, students and research teams onto one platform also allows innovators to present their work to a wider ecosystem.

How to apply for AIMM 2026

Interested startups, entrepreneurs, MSMEs, students and researchers can submit their applications online. The deadline is December 7, 2026.

Applicants can find further information and register through the AIMM 2026 application link.

With its focus on both early-stage concepts and revenue-generating products, the competition aims to connect AI innovation with problems that need practical solutions across manufacturing, industry and society.

item.title: 5 lessons from book Be Delusional by Harinder Singh Pelia
item.description: Discover five powerful lessons from Be Delusional by Harinder Singh Pelia on self-belief, ambition, confidence and turning big dreams into reality.
item.content:encoded:
What if believing in yourself before the world does is the first step towards achieving something extraordinary?

Most people wait for evidence before they start believing in their potential. They look for approval, reassurance and the right circumstances before pursuing ambitious goals. But what if the secret to success lies in believing that you are capable long before you have proof?

In Be Delusional: Bend Reality to Your Beliefs, author Harinder Singh Pelia explores how strong self-belief can influence ambition, behaviour and achievement. Drawing on psychology, real-life stories and practical exercises, the book challenges readers to question their limitations and develop the confidence to pursue seemingly impossible goals.

The book draws examples from personalities such as Sylvester Stallone, Lady Gaga and Kanye West, who believed in their abilities even when circumstances did not support their ambitions.

Here are five lessons to learn from Be Delusional that can change the way you approach your goals and ambitions.

5 lessons from Be Delusional by Harinder Singh Pelia

1. Believe in yourself before you have proof

One of the central ideas of the book is that successful people often believe in their abilities before they have anything to show for them. They do not necessarily wait for recognition, achievements or approval to develop confidence in themselves.

Consider Sylvester Stallone, who believed strongly in his potential as an actor despite facing rejection. Similarly, Lady Gaga continued pursuing her musical ambitions despite setbacks.

Their stories highlight an important lesson: confidence does not always come after success. Sometimes, it is what motivates people to work towards success in the first place.

The takeaway: Stop waiting for external validation to believe in your potential. Give yourself permission to pursue ambitions even when the results are uncertain.

2. Change the story you tell yourself

The way we describe ourselves can influence how we approach opportunities and challenges. If you constantly tell yourself that you are not talented enough, not experienced enough or not capable of achieving something, you may eventually start behaving as though those beliefs are facts.

Drawing on psychologist Dan McAdams' Narrative Identity Theory, Pelia explores how the stories people tell themselves contribute to their sense of identity.

Changing your internal narrative does not mean ignoring your weaknesses. It means refusing to let your past experiences become permanent definitions of who you are.

The takeaway: Instead of repeatedly telling yourself why you cannot achieve something, start building a narrative around the person you want to become.

3. Act like the person you want to become

Believing in a future version of yourself is important, but belief becomes meaningful when it influences your behaviour.

The book introduces a concept called the 'Lie Ladder', which describes different levels of belief and the behaviours associated with them. At the third level, a person begins acting like their desired future self in specific situations rather than simply thinking about their ambitions.

For instance, someone who wants to become a successful entrepreneur can start making decisions, building skills and taking responsibilities that align with that identity.

You do not have to wait until you achieve your goal to begin developing the habits associated with it.

The takeaway: Do not just visualise your future self. Start behaving like that person through small, consistent actions.

4. Stop letting other people's doubts define you

Ambitious goals often invite criticism, especially when they seem unrealistic to others. Friends, colleagues and even family members may question your decisions because they cannot see the possibilities you imagine.

However, other people's opinions do not necessarily determine what you are capable of achieving.

The stories explored in Be Delusional demonstrate how some successful personalities continued believing in their abilities despite rejection and scepticism. Their conviction helped them persist when external circumstances offered little encouragement.

This does not mean ignoring constructive criticism. Instead, it means learning to distinguish between useful feedback and opinions that simply discourage you.

The takeaway: Listen to advice that helps you grow, but do not allow someone else's limited expectations to become your own.

5. Turn ambitious beliefs into action

There is a difference between imagining an extraordinary future and actively working towards it. Positive thinking alone cannot guarantee success. It needs to be supported by effort, preparation, commitment and the willingness to take risks.

Pelia's book makes this distinction through its combination of psychological insights, real-world examples and practical exercises. It encourages readers to move beyond passive dreaming and develop a stronger commitment to their ambitions.

Whether you want to build a business, pursue a creative career or achieve a personal milestone, your beliefs should influence the decisions you make today.

The takeaway: Let your ambitions shape your actions. Believe in possibilities, but put in the work required to make them real.

Final thoughts

Be Delusional: Bend Reality to Your Beliefs by Harinder Singh Pelia challenges the conventional idea that people need evidence of success before they can believe in themselves.

The book presents self-belief as something that can be developed through the stories we tell ourselves, the identities we build and the actions we take. Its central message is not about blindly ignoring reality but about refusing to let current circumstances dictate the limits of future possibilities.

Sometimes, the first person who needs to believe in your dreams is you. And perhaps, being a little unreasonable about what you can achieve is exactly what encourages you to take the first step.

item.title: Stage III cancer to 200+ startups: How Tej Chingtham built the Northeast’s first incubator
item.description: From a push for better startup support to mentoring 200+ ventures, Prof. (Dr.) Tej Chingtham is helping shape Northeast India’s startup ecosystem through AIC-SMUTBI.
item.content:encoded:
When young people from Northeast India approached Prof. (Dr.) Tej Chingtham with questions about starting a business, he did not always have the answers.

Many had returned from other parts of the country hoping to build something of their own, but the region lacked the support system they needed.

In a conversation with Shradha Sharma, Founder and CEO of YourStory & The Bharat Project, Tej Chingtham recalled how these interactions prompted him to look more closely at the region's startup ecosystem in 2016.

At the time, he was a computer science professor with no plans to run an incubation centre.

Yet, what began as an attempt to understand the challenges facing local entrepreneurs eventually led him to build one.

Today, he is the CEO of the Atal Incubation Centre - Sikkim Manipal University Technology Business Incubation Foundation (AIC-SMUTBI), which works with more than 200 startups. The wider Northeast ecosystem has grown to over 2,000 startups.

An idea to bring mentors to the Northeast

When Tej Chingtham travelled across the northeastern states in 2016, he found entrepreneurs and several isolated efforts to support them.

What was missing was a system that could bring these initiatives together and offer founders consistent guidance.

Mentors from cities such as Bengaluru and Delhi would visit the region, spend a few weeks or a month with entrepreneurs, and then leave. Chingtham felt these short visits could not provide the sustained support startups needed.

He began thinking about a model that would encourage mentors to spend more time in the region. His idea was to combine mentoring with tourism, giving experts an opportunity to explore the Northeast while helping local entrepreneurs build their businesses.

In 2018, he got the opportunity to establish what he describes as the Northeast's first incubation centre. The task was unfamiliar.

Chingtham had never visited an incubator or worked in one, and had to learn how to build the institution while putting its support systems in place.

The work began on September 27, 2018. A few months later, on December 12, Chingtham was diagnosed with stage III lung cancer. He continued treatment while working towards the centre's establishment. AIC-SMUTBI became operational in June 2019.

Building an ecosystem beyond one centre

Tej Chingtham's ambition was never limited to setting up an incubation centre in Sikkim. He wanted entrepreneurs across the Northeast to have access to the mentorship and support that were often easier to find in established startup hubs.

The incubator gradually expanded its collaborations across all eight northeastern states. Chingtham credits the people who supported the initiative, particularly those who helped bring entrepreneurs and local stakeholders together in their respective states.

Speaking with Shradha, he emphasised how the effort had grown beyond the work of one institution.

The region now has more than 2,000 startups, of which over 200 work with AIC-SMUTBI, according to him. This means the incubator is associated with roughly one in every 10 startups in the Northeast.

He sees considerable potential in the region's natural resources, biodiversity and local industries.

Even its geographical position, with all eight northeastern states sharing international borders, can offer opportunities for entrepreneurs who understand the local context.

His larger aim is to encourage young people to recognise what they can build at home. Rather than viewing the Northeast only as a place to leave in search of employment, he wants them to see it as a place where businesses can grow.

Why founders need customers and investors

Access to funding remains one of the challenges for startups in the region. Tej Chingtham says relatively few investors visit the Northeast, which often leaves entrepreneurs to focus on building a customer base and generating revenue to sustain their businesses.

He puts the five-year survival rate of startups supported by the incubator at around 80%. According to him, their focus on customers and sustainable operations, rather than chasing large valuations, has contributed to this outcome.

He believes the ecosystem needs more early-stage mentorship, particularly experts who can help founders validate their ideas before they establish a legal entity or begin navigating funding and policy requirements.

Policies that make investment easier could also encourage more capital to flow into the region.

Chingtham has suggested tax holidays for a defined period to attract investors.

During his conversation with Shradha, he summed up what the Northeast needs from the investment community with a phrase he returned to more than once: “More than venture capital, we need adventure capitalists.”

He wants investors to travel to the region, understand its opportunities and engage with businesses that may not be based in the country's familiar startup centres.

Helping the next generation build locally

Tej Chingtham believes the Northeast needs more startups relative to its population.

Reaching that point will require sustained mentorship, supportive policies and investors willing to explore opportunities beyond established markets.

He is also quick to point out that the incubator's journey has never been the work of one person. Its progress has depended on the people, institutions and partners who helped strengthen the startup ecosystem across the region.

His ambition goes beyond increasing the number of ventures associated with AIC-SMUTBI. He wants more young people to consider entrepreneurship a viable career and use the resources available in their own states to build businesses.

The incubator began with an attempt to answer a question that young entrepreneurs kept bringing to Chingtham: how could they build something in the Northeast?

Today, he is working to ensure that the next generation has a stronger support system and more reasons to find that answer at home.

item.title: Odisha startup BabyCue wins national challenge with its rapid diagnostic test for children
item.description: Odisha-based BabyCue wins first prize at the Tribal Business Conclave Open Grand Challenge for DiaCue, its rapid test for childhood diarrhoea.
item.content:encoded:
A child with diarrhoea may need antibiotics, but not every infection is bacterial.

Without a quick way to identify the cause, doctors often have to make treatment decisions before test results arrive. This can lead to unnecessary antibiotic use, particularly in areas where access to diagnostic facilities is limited.

Odisha-based healthtech startup BabyCue Private Limited is working to address this gap with DiaCue, a rapid diagnostic test designed to distinguish bacterial from non-bacterial infections in children under five.

The startup recently won first prize at the Tribal Business Conclave Open Grand Challenge, organised by the Ministry of Tribal Affairs in association with Startup India and the Department for Promotion of Industry and Internal Trade (DPIIT). The award carries a cash prize of Rs 5 lakh.

BabyCue Founder Manish Kumar Swain and Co-founder Saumyashree Swain received the award from President Droupadi Murmu at Rashtrapati Bhavan in New Delhi.

Building a diagnostic tool around a healthcare gap

BabyCue's journey towards developing DiaCue began with fieldwork in rural Odisha. According to the company, its founding team spent time at primary and community health centres during a BIRAC SPARSH Fellowship in 2022.

The team found that healthcare workers often had the clinical knowledge to treat patients but lacked access to diagnostic tools that could help them identify the cause of diarrhoeal infections quickly.

Conventional stool testing can take 24 to 48 hours, leaving doctors to make treatment decisions while waiting for results. In such situations, antibiotics may be prescribed even when an infection is not bacterial.

BabyCue began developing DiaCue in 2024 to address this problem.

The point-of-care test uses a rapid diagnostic format to help distinguish bacterial from non-bacterial diarrhoea. The company's website says the test delivers results in 15 to 20 minutes and is designed to work without complex laboratory equipment or cold-chain storage.

Taking diagnostics closer to underserved communities

The idea behind DiaCue is to make diagnostic support more accessible in healthcare settings that may not have advanced laboratory infrastructure.

By helping clinicians identify whether an infection is bacterial, the test aims to support more targeted treatment and reduce unnecessary antibiotic prescriptions.

This is particularly relevant for rural and tribal communities, where access to timely diagnostic facilities can be limited.

The national recognition adds to BabyCue's growing list of milestones. The company is incubated at KIIT Technology Business Incubator and has also received support from the Technology Development Board under the Department of Science and Technology for developing its rapid diagnostic platform.

With the Rs 5 lakh award, BabyCue has another opportunity to take its work forward. Its focus remains on making diagnostic solutions more accessible, so that a child's treatment does not have to depend on guesswork or delayed test results.

item.title: Space, sustainability, AI: test your business creativity with Edition 258 of our weekly quiz!
item.description: This insightful feature from YourStory tests and strengthens your business acumen! Here are 5 questions to kick off this 258th quiz. Ready?
item.content:encoded:
Lateral Sparks, the weekly quiz from YourStory, tests your domain knowledge, business acumen, and lateral thinking skills (see the previous edition here). In this 258th edition of the quiz, we present issues tackled by real-life entrepreneurs in their startup journeys.

What would you do if you were in their shoes? At the end of the quiz, you will find out what the entrepreneurs and innovators themselves actually did. Would you do things differently?

Check out YourStory’s Book Review section as well, with takeaways from over 355 titles on creativity and entrepreneurship, and our weekend PhotoSparks section on creativity in the arts.

Also Read
Year in Review: The great Indian consumer reset powered by protein, pickleball and micro-dramas

Q1: Space debris

The challenges of satellite servicing and removal of space debris are hampering the space ambitions of many nations. How can these problems be addressed?

Q2: Wastewater

Many factories have wastewater treatment, but need to reduce the energy and chemicals needed to clean water for reuse. Where is the entrepreneurial opportunity here?

Q3: Industrial chemicals

Many industries use fossil-derived raw materials, which are not sustainable in the long run from an environmental point of view. Where is the business opportunity here?

Also Read
Year in Review: Top 10 celebrity-backed ventures of 2025

Q4: Cleaning solutions

Many factories and commercial spaces entail jobs such as cleaning that are repetitive and physically demanding. How can technology help here?

Q5: Digital impact

Enterprise software becomes more valuable when it understands not just the task it has been asked to perform, but the context behind it. How can this business benefit be realised in areas like marketing?

Answers!

Congratulations on having come this far! But there’s more to come – answers to these five questions (below), as well as links to articles with more details on the entrepreneurs’ solutions. Happy reading, happy learning – and happy creating!

A1: Space debris

Founded by Chiranjeevi Phanindra, Cosmoserve Space has built a facility to design, build, test, and operate systems for satellite servicing and space debris recovery. Of the approximately 28,000 satellites in orbit, nearly 10,000 are estimated to be dead or non-operational.

Eyeing this space, Cosmoserve also supports satellite servicing, including in-orbit repairs and refuelling. Read more here about its recent fundraise from Rebright Partners, Aranya Holdings, and Naandi Ventures.

A2: Wastewater

Founded by Mrityunjay Sahu, Bariflo Cybernetics combines sensors, AI software and automation to improve wastewater treatment processes. It has IoT sensors to monitor parameters such as pH, total dissolved solids, and flow.

Its AI models use the readings to determine chemical dosage and treatment processes at different stages. Read more here about this technology which can reduce energy consumption by approximately 25% and improve the efficiency of chemical use.

Also Read
Breaking barriers in 2025: Women’s progress at work and what the road ahead demands

A3: Industrial chemicals

Founded by Apoorv Garg and Yugal Raj Jain, altM uses biomass, including sugarcane bagasse and rice straw, to produce industrial chemicals. This helps the manufacturing sector move away from fossil-derived inputs in sectors such as textiles, construction and packaging.

“We are building a new source of industrial carbon from agricultural residue,” Garg says. Read more here about its recent fundraise from Rainmatter by Zerodha, Mela Ventures, Omnivore, and Spectrum Impact.

A4: Cleaning solutions

Founded by Runal Dahiwade, Peppermint Robotics makes a range of autonomous cleaning robots. They are deployed in factories, hospitals, airports, malls, warehouses, hotels, and universities.

They are particularly effective in physically-demanding settings such as healthcare and hospitality. Read more here about its recent fundraise from pi Ventures, Crane Venture Partners, and Asiana Fund.

Also Read
How IIT Madras Incubation Cell is powering India’s next-gen deeptech startups

A5: Digital impact

“Every brand now has access to the same AI. What it does not have is the same understanding of its customers,” explains Karthik Venkateswaran, Co-founder of Zocket. The startup helps businesses turn their own data and results into an AI that keeps getting smarter.

It helps deliver marketing that is agentic and context-rich via tools like Brand Brain. Read more here about how this integrated workflow brings consumer intelligence and performance signals into a shared context layer for specialised AI marketing capabilities.

YourStory has also published the pocketbook ‘Proverbs and Quotes for Entrepreneurs: A World of Inspiration for Startups’ as a creative and motivational guide for innovators.

item.title: Measure AI by results, not number of agents deployed: Oracle senior executive
item.description: Business leaders should pick an outcome they can measure, such as reducing the time spent resolving accounting errors or lowering transport costs, said, Natalia Rachelson, Senior Vice President, Applications Development, Oracle.
item.content:encoded:
Businesses adopting artificial intelligence (AI) should start with a measurable goal and judge success by the improvement it delivers rather than the number of AI agents deployed, as the technology moves from helping employees to doing work for them, a senior Oracle executive said.

"It’s important to remember that the number of agents deployed matters less than the improvement they deliver," Natalia Rachelson, Senior Vice President, Applications Development at Oracle, told PTI.

Business leaders should pick an outcome they can measure, such as reducing the time spent resolving accounting errors or lowering transport costs, she said.

"It’s important to establish a baseline first so you can assess whether AI is making a meaningful difference," she noted.

Companies then need to get the basics right: reliable data, clear ownership of processes, appropriate controls, and employees who understand how to work with AI agents. The biggest gains come from parts of a process where work gets delayed or needs repeated manual intervention, she said.

The biggest misconception business leaders have, she said, is that AI is about doing the same work faster.

"The biggest misconception is when people think that AI is about doing the same things faster, better, and cheaper. It is not. It is really about redefining how work gets done...If instead of 10,000 steps, you’re now down to five steps because AI does everything in the middle, that's a redefinition of a business process," she said.

Earlier AI tools focused largely on answering questions, drafting content and making recommendations, Rachelson said. Newer AI agents can coordinate the next steps and carry out authorised actions within a business process.

A company aiming to raise its customer renewal rate by 2 percent, for instance, could set it as a goal, and a team of specialised AI agents would analyse the data, come up with a plan and carry it out, she said.

In a hospital system, AI could schedule nurses with different specialisations and shifts. If a nurse calls in sick, it can redraw the schedule and alert the people who will fill in, she said.

The quickest results are likely in routine processes where teams spend a lot of time gathering information and chasing follow-ups, she said. In finance, AI agents can help reconcile accounts before the books are closed. In human resources, they can flag potential payroll issues. In supply chains, they can compare shipping options or work out how to allocate scarce materials, with teams reviewing and approving the plans.

People remain in charge throughout, Rachelson said.

"Enterprises need to define what an agent is allowed to do, how its work will be checked, and when a person needs to approve or intervene."

Rachelson, who has been with Oracle for about 15 years, said AI was a bigger shift than the move to cloud computing, but the questions it raises are familiar.

"AI is bigger than the cloud, but it’s no different. Every technology transition raises a lot of questions and concerns," she said.

She recalled the fears around Y2K, the computer date bug at the turn of the millennium, when "the world was coming to an end and then absolutely nothing happened".

item.title: 5 Lessons from Yoshuku: The Japanese Art of Manifesting
item.description: Discover five powerful lessons from Yoshuku by Azumi Uchitani on gratitude, manifestation, resilience, positive thinking, and intentional living.
item.content:encoded:
What if you could celebrate your dreams before they actually come true? Most people wait for success, happiness, or achievements before allowing themselves to celebrate. But what if celebrating in advance could change the way you approach your goals?

In Yoshuku: The Japanese Art of Manifesting, Azumi Uchitani introduces readers to the Japanese concept of Yoshuku, which means pre-celebration. It is a practice of expressing gratitude and celebrating a desired future as though it has already happened.

The book combines Japanese wisdom, traditional rituals, gratitude, and collective intention to show how we can create a more meaningful relationship with our dreams. It also reminds us that personal growth is not always about achieving something; it is about appreciating the journey along the way.

5 Important lessons to learn from Yoshuku by Azumi Uchitani.

1. Celebrate your dreams before they come true

The central idea of Yoshuku is to celebrate your desired future before it becomes reality. Instead of waiting for success to arrive, practise feeling grateful and excited about the possibilities ahead.

For example, if you dream of starting your own business, imagine celebrating its success with the people who supported you. This helps you develop a positive connection with your goals and gives you something meaningful to work towards.

The lesson is to enjoy the anticipation of your dreams rather than making happiness dependent entirely on their achievement.

2. Gratitude makes you appreciate what you already have

We often spend so much time thinking about what we want next that we forget to appreciate what we already have.

The book highlights Kansha, the Japanese concept of appreciation and gratitude. It encourages readers to recognise the people, experiences, and opportunities that make their lives meaningful.

Practising gratitude does not mean giving up on your ambitions. It means learning to appreciate your present while remaining hopeful about your future.

3. Difficult experiences help you grow stronger

One of the beautiful ideas explored in the book is the connection between personal growth and nature. Uchitani uses the image of cherry blossoms flourishing after powerful storms to explain how hardships can help us develop stronger roots.

Life does not always go according to plan. We experience disappointments, unexpected changes, and moments when moving forward feels difficult.

However, these experiences can teach us patience, resilience, and strength. Instead of seeing every setback as a failure, learn to recognise the opportunities for growth within difficult situations.

Also Read
Japan's Guide to Living Beautifully: Embrace Your Cracks with Kintsugi

4. Share your dreams and celebrate together

Manifestation does not always have to be a private journey. The book introduces the importance of collective intention and shared celebrations.

When you share your dreams with supportive people, you create opportunities for encouragement, connection, and mutual motivation.

Celebrating together also reminds us that success is not just about individual achievements. It can become more meaningful when the people around us are part of the journey.

5. Turn your intentions into daily actions

Having dreams and imagining a better future are important, but meaningful change also requires consistent effort.

The book encourages readers to create daily rituals that support their intentions. Whether it is practising gratitude in the morning, setting aside time for personal growth, or taking small steps towards a career goal, everyday actions help you stay connected to your vision.

Rather than constantly waiting for the perfect moment, focus on what you can do today to move closer to the life you want.

Final thoughts

Yoshuku: The Japanese Art of Manifesting by Azumi Uchitani offers a refreshing perspective on manifestation by introducing the idea of celebrating the future while appreciating the present.

Its lessons on gratitude, resilience, collective energy, and daily rituals remind us that the journey towards our dreams deserves as much attention as the final destination.

The biggest takeaway is that you do not have to wait until everything falls into place to experience happiness. Learn to celebrate small victories, appreciate the present, and welcome the future with hope and intention.

item.title: How the art ecosystem opens up a wide range of opportunities beyond creation of artworks
item.description: In this photo essay, we showcase more highlights from Chennai’s Contemporary Now arts festival, along with director insights.
item.content:encoded:
Launched in 2014, PhotoSparks is a weekly feature from YourStory, with photographs that celebrate the spirit of creativity and innovation. In the earlier 1,030 posts, we featured an art festival, cartoon gallery. world music festival, telecom expo, millets fair, climate change expo, wildlife conference, startup festival, Diwali rangoli, and jazz festival.

The third edition of the art festival 'Contemporary Now' wrapped up recently across 10 venues in Chennai. The artist lineup included Garima Gupta, Vishwa Shroff, Parag Tandel, Ayesha Sultana, Julien Segard, Chanakya School, Pushpakanthan Pakkiyarajah, Sakshi Gupta, Moumita Das, and many others.

The art festival’s directors, Ashvin Rajagopalan and Priyanjoli Basu, shared with YourStory a number of insights on trends, opportunities and tips for aspiring artists and entrepreneurs.

“There are many opportunities opening up in the art ecosystem. I think the market is professionalising. People are now creating fairly complex artworks,” Rajagopalan observes.

This calls for sales teams, social media marketing, and pubic relations. “The activities depend on the kinds of institutions and galleries involved,” he adds.

“These models exist well outside India, and include foundations and CSR projects. This is relatively new in India, where there is less institutional support for the arts,” he says.

Also Read
Year in review: startups that raised big from VCs in 2025

Fortunately, many private galleries and art collectors are coming up with their own spaces to showcase art. “Along with sales, we have exhibition designers, curators, production teams, and art handlers,” Basu explains, pointing to new emerging art roles.

“So there is a whole gamut of professions that is opening up. More such arts management roles and teaching institutions are called for,” she urges.

These are important conversations to have in order to nurture a sustainable art ecosystem. “There is a lot of on-the-job training that is happening, but more academic and vocational support is needed to sustain art professions and incomes,” Basu advises.

A wide range of practical, creative, administrative, and financial support roles are needed for a vibrant art ecosystem. They help create opportunities for artists to develop their work, exhibit their creations, connect with audiences, and build successful careers within the art industry.

For example, an art technician supports artists and galleries by preparing, installing and maintaining artwork. This includes framing, lighting, mounting, and setting up exhibitions, ensuring that artwork is displayed safely and professionally.

A gallery assistant helps with the daily running of an art gallery. Their responsibilities include welcoming visitors, answering questions, organising exhibitions, handling enquiries, and keeping the gallery organised and presentable.

Also Read
How IIT Madras Incubation Cell is powering India’s next-gen deeptech startups

An arts administrator helps with organising events, managing schedules, handling paperwork, communicating with artists, and supporting the planning of projects. Exhibition designers plan how artwork is presented within a gallery or exhibition space, and specialise in positioning of artwork to create an engaging experience for visitors.

An art conservator specialises in preserving and restoring artwork to prevent damage and deterioration. They use specialist knowledge and techniques to repair paintings, sculptures and other artworks while maintaining their original appearance and historical value.

Outreach officers help make art accessible to different audiences, including schools and local communities. They organise workshops, educational activities and creative programmes that encourage people to engage with art and develop their own artistic skills.

An art handler is responsible for carefully packing, moving, transporting and installing artwork. They ensure that valuable or fragile pieces are handled securely, particularly when artwork is being moved between studios, galleries and exhibitions.

Fundraising officers help art organisations and individual creative projects secure financial support. They apply for grants, organise fundraising events, approach potential sponsors, and develop relationships with organisations that can provide financial assistance to artists.

Mature art ecosystems keep up with shifts in the market and create trends as well. Among emerging trends in art, Rajagopalan points to the rise of AI as well as increasing demand for the handmade. “AI is a useful tool to generate ideas,” he says.

Also Read
Year in review: What 2025’s data tells us about women in India

As for tips for aspiring artists, Rajagoplan advises creators to find a gallery that they can relate to. Basu suggests spending more time in artist communities.

“Such communities foster an exchange of ideas and help create more art. While social media can seem attractive, it is also distractive,” she cautions.

Being part of a supportive art community allows artists to connect with people who have similar interests and passions. This creates a sense of belonging and encourages artists to feel more confident about their work.

Through community workshops, classes, demonstrations, and group activities, artists can experiment with different materials and techniques. In open communities, more experienced artists can share their knowledge with beginners, helping them improve and discover new ways of working.

Furthermore, art communities offer emotional support and encouragement. This can be especially important for artists who may experience self-doubt, creative blocks or difficulties in their careers.

The creative journey is full of ups and downs, twists and turns. Being surrounded by supportive people allows artists to discuss challenges, share experiences and receive constructive criticism.

Also Read
Year in Review: Top 10 celebrity-backed ventures of 2025

Positive feedback and encouragement can help artists overcome setbacks and feel motivated to keep pursuing their creative interests. It also reminds them that they are not alone in their artistic journey.

Art communities benefit the wider public as well. Community art projects, collaborative exhibitions and public workshops allow artists to work together and make a positive contribution to society.

Now what have you done today to pause in your busy schedule and harness your creative side for a better world?

(All photographs taken by Madanmohan Rao on location at 'Contemporary Now' venues in Chennai.)

item.title: Zomato-parent Eternal reworking 2030 EV delivery target amid fleet expansion, EV adoption
item.description: The company is working towards a revised timeline, factoring in the availability of electric vehicles, supporting government policies, and the transportation requirements of its various businesses.
item.content:encoded:
While remaining committed to green mobility, Zomato and Blinkit parent Eternal is reassessing its 2030 target for a 100% electric delivery fleet due to rapid business expansion and an evolving EV ecosystem.

In an interview with PTI, Anjalli Ravi Kumar, Chief Sustainability Officer at Eternal, said the company is working towards a revised timeline, factoring in the availability of electric vehicles (EVs), supporting government policies, and the transportation requirements of its various businesses.

"We are still committed to electrifying the fleet. We are deeply committed to it because it still makes economic sense," she said.

However, acknowledging that the earlier deadline may not be achievable, Kumar said the company's operations had expanded considerably since the original target was set.

"It doesn't look feasible because, beyond the penetration numbers, our business is also growing massively. When we set the target, there were only 1.5 lakh monthly active riders on Zomato. Today, there are 12 lakh riders across Zomato and Blinkit," she said.

On whether the company could commit to a revised target, possibly by 2035, Kumar said it was working towards a date, with the pace of EV policy implementation also likely to influence the decision.

"We are actively working towards a date. Some of it will depend on the government as well, in terms of whether EV policies have rolled out across the country sufficiently for us to commit to 2035. We are very hopeful. But bear in mind that we have other businesses as well.

“For instance, Hyperpure also uses a lot of delivery vehicles, and those are four-wheeler deliveries involving trucks and smaller commercial vehicles. So, the new EV target for the Eternal Group needs to factor in all kinds of transportation, not just the two-wheeler segment. We can't think about individual businesses anymore. When we set a target, we have to set it for the group. That's our thinking," she said.

Despite the challenges, the company said its delivery fleet was already seeing higher EV adoption than the broader Indian two-wheeler market. Kumar said the company's approach was to encourage partners to adopt EVs through financial incentives, greater access to rental options and awareness initiatives, rather than mandate a particular vehicle choice.

"In our previous estimation, which was done around last December, EV penetration in the market was only around 6-7%. Within our own fleet, there were already about 12-13% of partners using EVs. So, we were already at almost double the market penetration," she said.

One measure encouraging EV adoption is Zomato's equal-benefit policy, under which delivery partners using EVs are paid as much as those using petrol-powered vehicles, despite the lower operating costs.

Kumar said the company also facilitates access to EVs through rental options on its delivery partner app and initiatives such as the EV Bazaar, which familiarises partners with different models available in the market.

At the same time, she said, the scale of its delivery operations makes access and affordability important considerations, particularly as the company onboards large numbers of partners across cities.

"To maintain a base of 12 lakh riders a month, I need to onboard 30 lakh people a year. Now, the question is whether 30 lakh people across 900 cities will all be able to access an EV reliably.

“That's an important question, and this is just the number for this year. Tomorrow, it could be 35 lakh, right? Can I guarantee that all 30 lakh people joining us will have access to an EV across 900 cities? I'm not in a position to make that guarantee, and I don't know when I will," she said.

Kumar also stressed the importance of designing EV policies that account for the livelihoods and financial circumstances of delivery partners, who generally arrange their own vehicles.

She added that the company was advocating worker-friendly EV policies to ensure that the transition to cleaner mobility did not restrict employment opportunities for people who may not be in a position to purchase EVs.

Beyond electric mobility, Eternal is also working with restaurant partners to encourage the adoption of sustainable packaging through initiatives such as PackSwitch, an interactive website that helps restaurants identify alternatives to plastic packaging based on the dishes they serve.

Kumar said the company was working to address three key barriers to the adoption of sustainable packaging—complexity, convenience and cost—by helping restaurants discover suitable alternatives, improve access to suppliers and connect with startups developing new solutions.

Through its Hyperpure business, the company sold more than 3,000 metric tonnes of sustainable packaging to 50,000 restaurants last year.

On the consumer front, more than 10,000 restaurants across over 400 cities have received Zomato's low-plastic packaging tag after the company verified that the packaging used for their main menu was sustainable in nature.

item.title: 28 Indian startups pitch air pollution solutions to VCs at AirEarth.org event
item.description: AirEarth.org hosted 28 Indian clean-air startups pitching to VCs like Blume and Rainmatter, pushing year-round pollution fixes.
item.content:encoded:
In India, air pollution tends to arrive as a seasonal story. Every winter, smog over the north makes headlines for a few weeks, and then attention moves on. The AirEarth.org Pitch & Partnership Event set out to treat it differently: as a year-round problem that businesses can solve, and that investors can back.

AirEarth.org is an India-based clean-air community and action platform. It brings together professionals, innovators, investors and citizens to tackle air pollution through technology, policy and capital.

The format was simple. Founders building on-ground clean-air solutions were put in the same room as active investors looking for practical climate-tech bets. The goal was to move promising ideas from pilots and proofs of concept towards scale.

Seven tracks, from clean energy to carbon markets

Pitches were grouped into seven tracks that map the main sources of India's dirty air: Clean Energy, Industry, Construction & Urban Air, Waste & Circularity, Carbon Markets & Emerging Solutions, Promising Solutions, and For Grants.

The last track is a nod to the fact that not every clean-air effort is a venture-scale business. Some community and non-profit initiatives need grant capital rather than equity, and the event made room for them too.

The 28 startups and initiatives in the room

The lineup ranged from clean fuels and EV infrastructure to circular packaging and air-cleaning technology. Alongside private companies were foundations and community-led efforts, such as utensil banks that replace disposable tableware at events.

The 28 participants were Agastya Hydrogen Private Limited, Airmobility Infra Private Limited, ambiAir Cleaning Technologies, Angirus Ind Pvt Ltd, Arak Bio Fuels Pvt Ltd, Avesa GreenDrive Private Limited (SwitchEko), Bakz4ever (OPC) Pvt. Ltd., DO Localz, Eco Saathi, EGEE PALLET PVT LTD, GreenCar, Green Sarthi + Sheetal Bartan Bank, GREENGOLD CARBON PRIVATE LIMITED, Kalki Ecosphere Pvt. Ltd., Kona, Mistify AI Technologies, Net Zero Initiative Private Limited (RenewCred), Newcycl (Rawbin), Novorbis Itus Ltd, Rise Foundation, STEPUPIFY, SUSintel, Suspack Technologies Pvt Ltd, Thatsmyev.com, TRINANO TECHNOLOGIES PVT LTD, Vaidic Srijan LLP, VPA ONE POWER INDIA and Why Waste Wednesdays Foundation.

The investors at the table

Nine VCs and funds took part in the pitch sessions: 247VC, A Square Capital, AWE Funds, Blume Ventures, IAN Group, Rainmatter VC, Small Ticket Finance, Thinkuvate and Zeca Capital. The mix spans early-stage generalists, climate-focused capital and lenders writing smaller cheques.

That range matters for this sector. Many clean-air businesses, such as fuel switching, waste processing or retrofits for industry, need a blend of equity, debt and patient capital rather than a single large venture round.

Why it matters: clean air as a market, not a season

Public debate on air quality usually centres on bans, emergency measures and blame. Those spikes in attention rarely translate into steady funding for the companies doing the slow work of cutting emissions at the source.

By linking founders solving hard, on-ground environmental problems with investors who can help them grow, AirEarth.org is making the case for year-round, market-driven answers to India's air quality challenge.

The bet is that clean air will improve faster when the solutions behind it are viable businesses, not one-off campaigns.

item.title: How art exhibitions provide unmatched experiences of aesthetics, scale and technique
item.description: In this photo essay from Lalit Kala Akademi in New Delhi, we showcase more highlights from its annual national art exhibition.
item.content:encoded:
Launched in 2014, PhotoSparks is a weekly feature from YourStory, with photographs that celebrate the spirit of creativity and innovation. In the earlier 1,030 posts, we featured an art festival, cartoon gallery. world music festival, telecom expo, millets fair, climate change expo, wildlife conference, startup festival, Diwali rangoli, and jazz festival.

At the 65th National Exhibition of Art organised by Lalit Kala Akademi (LKA) in New Delhi, 20 artists were conferred with awards. The artists include Sanjay Kumar Sahani, Sanjib Kumar Gogoi, Santa Deb, Siddharth Shahjirao Shingade, Usharanjan Mandal, and Vijendra Sharma.

Sanjay Kumar Sahani is a contemporary visual artist who draws attention to youth as a subject of artistic reflection. He explores themes of their identity, energy and daily experiences.

Sanjib Kumar Gogoi is known for his engagement with figurative and abstract painting, distinctive textural effects, and antique-inspired artistic styles. He completed his MFA in painting at Rabindra Bharati University, Kolkata, and has more than two decades of artistic practice.

Santa Deb is a contemporary sculptor whose artistic practice exemplifies simplicity, balance and the aesthetic qualities of form. Siddharth Shahjirao Shingade and Usharanjan Mandal experiment with mixed-media techniques and alternative artistic materials, while Vijendra Sharma has made a mark as a contemporary painter.

Wide exposure to such artists helps visitors appreciate different cultural traditions, identities and perspectives. The diversity of painting, sculpture, printmaking, drawing, and mixed-media works shows viewers how similar themes can be expressed in a multitude of ways, as highlighted in this photo essay.

Also Read
2026 Outlook: AI, robotics, biotech, unicorns and the road ahead

Viewing original artworks inspires audiences to think creatively and develop their own imagination. By addressing subjects such as environmental protection and urban life, they connect aesthetics and activism.

The blend of the traditional and the contemporary shows that India's artistic heritage is a font of inspiration and motivation. This applies to artists, art enthusiasts, collectors, historians, students, and members of the public.

Observing the excellence of professional artworks spurs aspiring creators in their own artistic journeys. Books and digital media are popular sources of knowledge about art – but art exhibitions provide unique opportunities to experience and engage with art.

Exhibitions allow audiences to experience the actual size, dimensions and physical impact of artworks, particularly large paintings and installations. It encourages them to consider ideas and viewpoints they may not have previously encountered.

Exhibitions also provide opportunities to encounter artists whose work may not be widely available in books or online platforms. This helps audiences discover new talent and creative approaches.

Seen up close and from different angles, visitors can examine brushstrokes, layering, textures, materials, and techniques. This helps in gaining a deeper understanding of how artworks are actually created, and appreciating the perseverance and discipline required for artists.

Also Read
Year in review: startups that raised big from VCs in 2025

Seeing an exhibition along with other visitors, artists, curators, and art professionals makes art a shared cultural experience. The arrangement, lighting and surroundings of an exhibition create an immersive experience that digital images cannot fully reproduce.

Art exhibitions offer audiences a direct, interactive and sensory experience that extends beyond simply looking at images. This leads to deeper ways of understanding and appreciating art.

In the case of a pan-India exhibition of art, viewing original artworks from different regions provides a stronger appreciation of the country's diverse cultural identities. This extends to regional traditions, religious influences and artistic heritage.

In sum, the 65th National Exhibition of Art by LKA is a national snapshot of contemporary Indian visual art. The showcased artworks were selected from 6,175 submissions of 2,495 artists across 27 States and Union Territories.

It is therefore significant not just as an exhibition in the capital, but as one of the Akademi's principal mechanisms for identifying, recognising and giving national visibility to India's emerging and established visual artists.

Now what have you done today to pause in your busy schedule and harness your creative side for a better world? 

(All photographs taken by Madanmohan Rao on location at Lalit Kala Akademi.)

item.title: How Tej Chingtham built Northeast’s first incubator; The pilot-turned-entrepreneur who is building a wellness brand
item.description: In a conversation with Shradha Sharma, Founder and CEO of YourStory and The Bharat Project, Prof Tej Chingtham, CEO of Atal Incubation Centre - Sikkim Manipal University Technology Business Incubation Foundation, recalls what led him to look at the Northeast's startup ecosystem closely.
item.content:encoded:
Dear Reader,

How should AI be measured? Should the focus be on the number of agents deployed?

Natalia Rachelson, Senior Vice President, Applications Development, Oracle, believes the number of agents matters less than the improvement they deliver. She says business leaders should pick outcomes they can measure, such as reducing time spent resolving accounting errors or lowering transport costs. 

While impact matters, so does responsible usage. 

India’s markets regulator Sebi will soon issue detailed guidelines for responsible use of AI in the capital markets. 

Sebi chairman Tuhin Kanta Pandey said the proposed guidelines would focus on establishing appropriate guardrails for AI use, including disclosures, accountability of regulated entities, and a ‘human-in-the-loop’ approach. 

Moving on, Zomato-parent Eternal is reassessing its 2030 target for a 100% electric delivery fleet due to rapid business expansion and an evolving EV ecosystem.

Anjalli Ravi Kumar, Chief Sustainability Officer at Eternal, said the company is working towards a revised timeline, factoring in availability of electric vehicles, supporting government policies, and the transportation requirements of its various businesses.

In other news, India and the US have already agreed that Indian goods in the American market will receive preferential market access compared to competitor nations, Commerce and Industry Minister Piyush Goyal told media in Cairo. India and the US finalised the framework for the first phase of the bilateral trade agreement in February. 

ICYMI: Here’s the video of SpaceX’s Starship’s incredible return to the launch pad from orbit.

In today’s newsletter, we will talk about 

  • How Tej Chingtham built Northeast’s first incubator
  • The pilot-turned-entrepreneur who is building a wellness brand 

Here’s your trivia for today: What is the rare economic condition when rising prices and recession occur at once? (Scroll down for the answer)

Startup Ecosystem

How Tej Chingtham built Northeast’s first incubator

When young people from Northeast India approached Prof (Dr) Tej Chingtham with questions about starting a business, he did not always have the answers. In a conversation with Shradha Sharma, Founder and CEO of YourStory and The Bharat Project, Dr Chingtham recalled how these interactions prompted him to look more closely at the region’s startup ecosystem in 2016.

What began as an attempt to understand the challenges that local entrepreneurs faced eventually led him to build an incubation centre. He battled stage III lung cancer while working towards the centre’s establishment. Today, he is the CEO of the Atal Incubation Centre - Sikkim Manipal University Technology Business Incubation Foundation, which works with more than 200 startups. The wider Northeast ecosystem has grown to over 2,000 startups. 

Key takeaways 

  • Dr Tej Chingtham believes the Northeast needs more startups relative to its population. Reaching that point will require sustained mentorship, supportive policies, and investors willing to explore opportunities beyond established markets.
  • Dr Chingtham’s ambition was never limited to setting up an incubation centre in Sikkim. He wanted entrepreneurs across the Northeast to have access to the mentorship and support that were often easier to find in established startup hubs.
  • He wants more young people to consider entrepreneurship as a viable career and use the resources available in their own states to build businesses at home. Rather than viewing the Northeast as a place to leave in search of employment, he wants youngsters to see it as a place where businesses can grow.

Inspiration

This pilot-turned-entrepreneur is building a wellness brand for women

After a decade flying for IndiGo, Natasha Chaudhary turned to her own experiences with hormonal changes to launch Everyday You, a wellness brand for women navigating the health concerns that come with middle age. The brand has been built on the premise that women don’t have to suffer through it.

Key takeaways

  • Everyday You blends Ayurveda and modern science, bringing together ingredients such as magnesium, ashwagandha, chasteberry and shatavari in a single formulation. 
  • The brand has launched two products so far. Everyday Balance is a hormonal wellness blend that targets mood, anxiety, sleep, and night sweats. The second product, Everyday De-Bloat, is a natural solution for post-meal bloating, indigestion, and period bloat. 
  • In the crowded market of nutraceuticals riding on rising awareness around perimenopause and menopause, Natasha is betting on a more cautious message: women do not need everything on the shelf. “I’m putting myself out there and saying that what helped me can help you as well,” she says.

News & updates

  • US-China talks: US President Donald Trump will meet Chinese President Xi Jinping this week with a key part ​of his trade strategy unfinished: securing a homegrown supply of critical minerals to counter Beijing’s dominance. China is expected to use its dominance in rare earths as a negotiating tool.
  • Ageing systems: A massive, nearly five-hour shutdown of the US aviation system that has disrupted more than 20,000 flights since Friday may have been the fault of a single router installed by government contractor L3Harris, government officials said. The incident is the latest example of the ageing US air traffic control telecom system ​and the struggles to replace systems while keeping the old communications working. 
  • Alice Huang: Megaspeed has said that Chinese businesswoman Alice Huang, whose ties ​to former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang have raised US national ‌security concerns, officially left the company on August 30, 2025, and has no current role there. 

What you should watch out for

Bengaluru Tech Summit: The 29th edition of the Bengaluru Tech Summit runs from November 17 to 19 at BIEC under the theme ‘AI & Beyond’, bringing together the global technology ecosystem to explore AI and the breakthrough technologies shaping the future. 

What is the rare economic condition when rising prices and recession occur at once?

Answer: Stagflation
